title: Adjuvant Larotrectinib in a Resected Secretory Carcinoma-Like Lung Adenocarcinoma Harboring EML4-NTRK3 Fusion: Case Report
author: Vladmir Cláudio Cordeiro de Lima; Breno Jeha Araújo; Felipe D' Almeida Costa; Beatriz Fuga Rossi Teixeira; André Luiz Cicilini; Carolina de Bustamante Fernandes; Juliana Folador Morellato; Rodrigo Dienstmann; Mariana Tosello Laloni
text:
Abstract
Secretory carcinoma of the lung is an exceptionally rare salivary gland-type malignancy, typically associated with NTRK fusions. We report a 71-year-old woman with pulmonary stage IIIA adenocarcinoma having salivary gland differentiation and solid-cribriform architecture, confirmed by S100 and Pan-TRK immunohistochemistry. Broad DNA and RNA next-generation sequencing identified an EML4-NTRK3 fusion. After adjuvant chemotherapy, maintenance larotrectinib was initiated based on proven TRK inhibitor efficacy in metastatic NTRK-fusion tumors and emerging evidence for targeted therapy benefit in driver-positive early stage lung adenocarcinoma. Our findings demonstrate the value of molecular pathology in the diagnostic journey of pulmonary malignancies, guiding rare fusion detection and supporting therapeutic decisions based on rare fusions in early stage disease.
Keywords: Secretory carcinoma, NSCLC, NTRK fusion, Larotrectinib, Case report
Introduction
Primary lung malignancies with salivary gland type differentiation represent a histologically diverse group, including mucoepidermoid carcinomas (MECs), adenoid cystic carcinomas (ACCs), pulmonary acinic cell carcinoma, pleomorphic adenoma, epithelial-myoepithelial carcinomas (EMECs), hyalinizing clear cell carcinoma, oncocytomas, and secretory carcinoma of the lung (salivary duct-like carcinoma).1,2 Secretory salivary duct-like carcinoma of the lung (SCL) is exceptionally rare, with only case reports documented. It is postulated to arise from submucosal salivary glands of the main tracheobronchial tree and may be morphologically indistinguishable from salivary gland tumors of the head and neck.1,3,4
Salivary gland type tumors (SGTTs) appear to be enriched for NTRK rearrangements, particularly the ETV6-NTRK3 gene fusion, although prevalence varies across case series.5,6 The EML4-NTRK3 fusion, by contrast, may be present in less than 1% of NSCLCs.6,7 Selective tropomyosin receptor kinase inhibitors (TRKis), such as larotrectinib and entrectinib, have demonstrated efficacy in metastatic NSCLC and are recommended first-line palliative therapies for patients with advanced cancer with oncogenic NTRK fusions.5,8
We report the case of a 71-year-old woman with a history of luminal breast cancer and a 20-pack-year smoking history (abstinent for 6 y) who was diagnosed with stage III, high-grade lung adenocarcinoma exhibiting salivary gland differentiation harboring an EML4-NTRK3 fusion and is currently undergoing adjuvant larotrectinib therapy. This case highlights both diagnostic challenges in classifying SGDTs and the therapeutic implications of detecting rare NTRK fusions in lung adenocarcinoma.
Case Report
A 71-year-old white woman, psychologist, with Eastern Cooperative Oncology Group score of 0, a 20 pack-year smoking history (abstinent for 6 y), and controlled dyslipidemia (on statin therapy) had a history of stage IIIC luminal breast cancer in 2019 (stage pT2pN3aM0). She underwent adjuvant chemotherapy with dose-dense doxorubicin/cyclophosphamide for 4 cycles and weekly paclitaxel for 12 weeks, followed by radiotherapy and endocrine therapy with anastrozole since 2020 (planned for 10 y), with no recurrence to date. She had two sisters diagnosed with breast cancer but tested negative for hereditary breast and ovarian cancer syndrome on germline testing for BRCA1 and BRCA2.
During breast cancer follow-up in September 2024, a previously stable 10-mm right lower lobe (RLL) pulmonary nodule demonstrated interval growth to 15 mm and increased FDG uptake (SUVmax 9.3) on positron emission tomography–computed tomography (PET-CT) compared with prior imaging. Figure 1A summarizes the patient diagnostic and therapeutic journey.
In November 2024, she underwent robotic-assisted surgical resection of the pulmonary lesion and mediastinal lymphadenectomy. Histopathology revealed a 1.8 × 0.6 cm carcinoma with solid cribriform and microcystic architecture, eosinophilic cytoplasm, and intraluminal secretions, strongly resembling secretory carcinoma of the salivary gland. Focally, there were also areas of micropapillary and complex gland formations. Both lymphovascular invasion and nodal metastases (stations 7 and 9) without capsular extravasation were documented, with final pathologic stage pT1cpN2bM0 (stage IIIA).
Immunohistochemistry (IHC) supported the diagnosis of pulmonary adenocarcinoma with areas resembling secretory carcinoma of salivary gland origin, revealing focal S100 and nuclear and cytoplasmic Pan-TRK expression (Fig. 1B), with concomitant diffuse TTF1 positivity and mammaglobin negativity (Table 1). Given secretory features and positive Pan-TRK expression, broad next-generation sequencing (NGS) was performed using the GS Infinity panel, an in-house validated assay analyzing 700 genes (SureSelect Agilent DNA and RNA panels), covering mutations, copy number alterations, fusions, tumor mutational burden, and microsatellite instability (MSI). Sequencing identified an EML4-NTRK3 fusion (exon 2–exon 14) (Fig. 1C), as illustrated in Figure 2, with low mutational burden (tumor mutational burden < 10 mut/Mb), mismatch repair proficient (pMMR). In addition, the tumor had PD-L1 expression tumor proportion score equals 20% (antibody 22C3).

Despite the negative hereditary breast and ovarian cancer panel, a larger germline NGS panel was pursued, identifying a heterozygous variant of uncertain significance (VUS) in the RECQL4 gene (c.736A>C; p.Ser246Arg).
The patient completed four cycles of adjuvant chemotherapy (carboplatin area under the curve 5 + paclitaxel 200 mg/m2 every 3 wk) in February 2025. A follow-up PET-CT (Fig. 1D) and brain magnetic resonance imaging revealed no evidence of disease.
Three weeks after completing chemotherapy, the patient started treatment with larotrectinib, 100 mg, twice daily. After 1 week, she developed dizziness and tinnitus, prompting a dose reduction to 100 mg once daily. The patient remains disease free in examinations performed in June 2025. The plan is to continue larotrectinib for 2 years, with imaging reassessment scheduled every 12 weeks.
Discussion
This report describes a rare case of high-grade SCL in an elderly female patient with tobacco exposure. Although this tumor type typically arises in head and neck salivary glands (e.g., submandibular, parotid, lips, thyroid) and has been previously characterized as a distinct entity in the breast (mammary analogue secretory carcinoma), primary pulmonary cases remain exceedingly rare (<0.1% of cases).2,4
The clinical presentation of SCL in our case exhibited several unusual features. First, although most reported cases have low-grade features,2,4 our patient presented with high-grade morphology. Second, although SGTTs typically occur between the fourth and fifth decades of life,1,2 our patient developed the disease at an older age. Third, given their presumed origin from tracheobronchial submucosal glands, SCL and most SGTTs typically present as central lesions causing obstructive symptoms (cough, dyspnea, hemoptysis), whereas our patient’s peripheral lesion remained asymptomatic.2,9 Tobacco exposure, a well-established risk factor for conventional lung neoplasms and certain SGTTs (particularly adenoid cystic carcinoma and hyalinizing clear cell carcinoma),1,9 may have contributed to tumorigenesis in this case.
SGTTs generally demonstrate favorable outcomes with 5-year overall survival more than 65%, though prognosis varies by histology.1,9 Qin et al.10 identified poor prognostic factors including the following: age above 58 years (OR = 2.42), tumor size more than 40 mm (OR = 1.51), metastatic disease (OR = 2.43), and high-grade histology (OR = 4.15). Staging follows the standard TNM classification for NSCLC. Most SGTTs present as localized disease.3 Elnayal et al.3 demonstrated that CT findings correlate with worse outcomes, whereas PET-CT avidity predicts nodal involvement without affecting survival. CT and PET-CT underestimated the true disease extent in this case. Because the lesion was peripheral and measured less than 3.0 cm, invasive mediastinal staging was not undertaken before surgery.3
IHC is crucial for distinguishing primary from metastatic disease, given histologic overlap with head and neck salivary tumors.1,4,9 Although classical secretory carcinomas have ETV6-NTRK3 positivity with GATA3 expression,4,11 our case demonstrated TTF1/S100/Pan-TRK positivity with GATA3 negativity, confirming pulmonary origin. Negative GATA-3, HER2, ER, and PR excluded breast cancer metastasis.
As previously noted, secretory carcinomas of salivary gland origin typically harbor ETV6-NTRK3 fusions,4,5 representing a critical therapeutic target for TKI. The observed Pan-TRK immunohistochemical expression suggested an underlying NTRK fusion, prompting NGS, which confirmed an EML4-NTRK3 gene fusion (exon 2–exon 14). NTRK fusions are rare genomic events, occurring in only approximately 0.3% of NSCLCs,6 with SQST-NTRK1, ETV-NTRK3, and SQSTM1-NTRK3 being the most frequently reported fusion variants.12
The EML4 (Echinoderm Microtubule-Associated Protein-Like 4)-NTRK3 fusion represents an exceptionally rare genomic alteration, although it is documented in secretory carcinomas. This chimeric protein typically retains NTRK3's kinase domain along with EML4's oligomerization domain, resulting in constitutive activation of oncogenic pathways (MAPK/ERK, PI3K/AKT, and PLCγ).8,12,13
A phase II basket trial evaluating larotrectinib in NTRK-fusion tumors demonstrated an intention-to-treat overall response rate of 75%, with 13% of patients achieving complete responses.13 In a separate phase II trial focusing exclusively on NSCLC, the response rate reached 73%, with a median duration of response of 33.9 months and progression-free survival of 35 months.14
Based on high pathologic risk of relapse, the patient received adjuvant chemotherapy. The decision to offer maintenance larotrectinib, the only TKI currently available in Brazil, was based on compelling efficacy and safety data for TKI in locally advanced and metastatic disease settings.5,12,13 Moreover, we anticipated that this patient could derive benefit from adjuvant larotrectinib similar to what was observed in the ALINA trial, where adjuvant alectinib was given to resected stage IB to IIIA, ALK-rearranged NSCLC, and resulted in a disease-free survival rate at 2 years of 93.8% in the alectinib group and 63.0% in the chemotherapy group (hazard ratio for disease recurrence or death at 0.24, p value < 0.001), respectively, for patients with stages II to IIIA.15 Of note, there are no studies evaluating the role of adjuvant larotrectinib in NTRK fusion-positive early stage lung cancer, and the TKI was offered in an off-label setting, with patient consent.
Conclusion
Primary salivary gland-type secretory carcinoma of the lung represents an exceptionally rare entity. The identification of NTRK gene fusions represents a critical therapeutic target as the available TRK inhibitors have demonstrated remarkable efficacy in metastatic NTRK-rearranged tumors across multiple histologies. Emerging evidence suggests that targeted therapies may similarly improve outcomes in early stage disease, as found in resected ALK-positive tumors. Our findings demonstrate the value of molecular pathology in the diagnostic journey of pulmonary malignancies, guiding rare fusion detection and supporting therapeutic decisions in early stage disease.
